captions.instagram:
How does cotton form?

Every white strand in a cotton boll is one single cell, grown nearly 3 cm long in twenty days, then filled with cellulose, dried and twisted. Grow one yourself, spin it into thread, and follow the fibre from Mehrgarh through empire, slavery and Gandhi's charkha to Bt cotton.

→ A cotton boll is a fruit, and every white strand in it is one single living cell.
→ From the day the flower opens, single seed cells grow to nearly 3 cm in about 20 days.
→ Then it stops growing and fills with cellulose, one daily layer at a time, spiralling as it goes.
→ The boll opens, the cell dies and dries, and the tube collapses into a twisted ribbon.
→ Cotton is glucose chains joined by hydrogen bonds. Water slips between the loose ones, so it drinks sweat and gets stronger wet.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/cottonclear (link in bio)

Every white strand in a cotton boll is one single cell, grown nearly 3 cm long in twenty days, then filled with cellulose, dried and twisted. Grow one yourself, spin it into thread, and follow the fibre from Mehrgarh through empire, slavery and Gandhi's charkha to Bt cotton.

⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/cottonclear

In this video:
• A seed hair, one cell long. Cotton is a shrub whose fruit, the boll, holds about 30 seeds.
• One cell, 3 cm long. From the day the flower opens, a seed-skin cell grows for about 20 days to 25 to 30 mm.
• Why cotton behaves as it does. Cellulose chains hold on by hydrogen bonds.
• Twist makes friction make strength. Gins take off the lint, about a third of seed cotton's weight.
• Growing it, fairly. India has the world's largest cotton area and is second in output, mostly grown on rain.
• A thread through history. Cotton threads at Mehrgarh date to the 6th millennium BCE.
